The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping doesn't just take us back to the arena, but also returns us to District 12 and the Covey population first introduced in Suzanne Collins's novel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.

Whitney Peak plays Lenore Dove Baird, the girlfriend of Joseph Zada's Haymitch Abernathy, and – as you might have guessed from her surname – a relation of Lucy Gray Baird, played by Rachel Zegler in the Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes film. The two women don't just share a name, either, but also a rebellious, free-spirited nature and a hatred for the Capitol.

GamesRadar+ sat down with the Sunrise on the Reaping cast in London, and we asked Peak if she drew inspiration from Zegler's Lucy Gray while crafting her own version of Lenore Dove.

"Absolutely," says Peak. "I think also just sort of setting the tone or looking for inspiration, listening to her sing was really great in getting me there. And then also, I think they're kind of strung together, just in Suzanne's writing. I think they share a lot of the same pieces, and so it's pretty good to just sort of refer back to the source material."

Lenore Dove's relationship with Haymitch is a bright spot for them both, though, naturally, tragedy lies ahead when Haymitch is reaped on his sixteenth birthday and forced to compete in the Second Quarter Quell, a more brutal edition of the deadly Hunger Games.

"It was so important to me to make that side of the film really happy and energetic, and just make it feel like nothing bad could happen, and have that love at the start of the film so the rest of the film works," Zada tells us of his first day shooting with Peak, in a scene featuring the young couple stealing a moment together in the Meadow, a green space on the outskirts of District 12. "And being able to work with Whitney and play that scene was fantastic. And also, it's just such a beautiful location as well."

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is in theaters this November 20. For more, check out our guide to all the most exciting upcoming movies left of 2026.

#3798. The Sunday Papers

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

While following a peculiar trail of silver and saffron leaves around the largest roots of the Treehouse, you come across a hexagonal wooden door lying half-hidden among ivy and moss. Scraping away the dirt, you discover a faint, absurd engraving of a newspaper. What mystery is here? You turn the brass knob – strange, it is warm! – and the engraving of the newspaper flutters. The pages turn faster and faster, emitting a howling gale that bowls you head over foot. When you pick yourself up, you are inside a vast attic full of books and bricabrac, lit from one side by windows that offer no view of the outside world – just light and mist.

Tarnation! You have been lured into the eternal prison of Sunday Afternoon. Fortunately, there are several ways to escape. Each of the arcane objects before you is secretly a portal, transporting you to another site of arcane activity, in a bizarre web of diversions that cannot possibly reflect the hand of a human curator. Which will you choose?

As you step forward, your toe nudges an ornamental scroll. It growls and wriggles like a panicking caterpillar, scooting away under a table. Before you lose sight of it, you discern the title and subject of the text – it's an essay by Kyle Tam about the yokai of Promise Mascot Agency.

Deep in a drawer, you discover a sour-smelling binder full of extracts from an ancient and all but indecipherable dispute over the discovery of "generative AI" in something called "Big Walk". The stakes are long-buried, but many of the individual pieces of writing are lively. Here is Bruno Dias noting in passing that "one of the harms of the 'AI' political project is the propaganda machine dedicated to making you feel stupid and helpless." Here is a professorial interjection from Brendan Keogh calling on the warring parties to recognise when "critiques of generative AI are actually just deflected critiques of the capitalist relations of technology and labour". Here is Mike Cook arguing that "what's happening is not unusual, it's not extreme, it's not unfair and it's not a 'public flogging'." Here is a ticker tape message from Hannah Nicklin observing that "if your radical position doesn’t have room for transformation it will not be safe until it contains just you".

A footnote in the same dusty sheaf of papers points you towards another work from Mike Cook in a different drawer. This one consists of neon slides, slotted into an antique View-Master, and explores a comparison between procedural generation and street photography.

Peering at the weirdly white and opaque windowpanes, you realise there are intricate equations traced in the condensation. It appears to be a post-mortem for a "post-cosy" game called Danchi Days, in which developer Melos Han-Tani discusses wishlist conversion rates and the problem of not fitting neatly into any recognisable genre.

A snowglobe stands on a mantelpiece, the flakes still orbiting a miniature washtub as though the object had been recently shaken, even though the chamber has clearly been abandoned for decades. You put it to your ear, anticipating the faint jingle of Xmas bells. Instead, you are almost deafened by a screeching guitar chord. Here is Erin Keane to explain.

Next to the snowglobe on the mantelpiece, there's a souvenir shop conch shell, polished to a high sheen. You put that to your ear, hoping to catch the soothing shuffle of surf on shingle, and a disembodied voice tells you to piss off. Tim Sniffen has some thoughts about gentrification, and why only he should be allowed to do it.

Again, one of these mystic artefacts hides the key to your release from the suffocating stillness of Sunday Afternoon. Which will you choose? Or have you, perhaps, brought a sorcerous teleportation device of your own? Please share. Here is Joanna Newsom's Cosmia to help you think.

World of Warcraft: Forever's having some teething issues with its new spellcaster itemisation. The idea, to sum it up quick, is that a lot of the power that was in spells innately has been pushed onto items, instead, with the intention to make it feel really good when you get a cool new staff as a mage, for instance.

This has had unintended consequences, as discovered by Rextroy (the same madlad who solos raid bosses), as shared on YouTube. The problem is this: Gear in Forever can give a lot of raw power to your healing and damage spells, as part of the aforementioned changes. But that raw power also applies to lower-level healing spells, too.

In Forever (and in Classic), casting lower-level spells is a core part of managing your mana as a healer. In this instance, however, "the healing coefficient on healing power remains the same, which is around 43% [on a low level Flash of Light], so if I stack all healing green items, I get my healing power up towards 242," Rextroy explains.

This, combined with the Paladin talent Oath of Light (which slaps another 61 healing onto Flash of Light), along with Spiritual Focus and Concentration Aura, which makes it almost impossible for enemies to interrupt or push-back the casting of his Flash of Light, and this makes his paladin basically unkillable.

The low-rank version of his Flash of Light spell doesn't cost enough mana to outpace his natural mana regeneration, it heals for a bunch because of his gear, and enemies can't slow or interrupt it. Which makes him almost unkillable.

I say almost, because as his experimentations prove, he can still become stunned or crowd-controlled by high-level enemies. And there are limitations. While he can stand up to a level 60 enemy whacking on him, add two or three to the mix and he can no longer outpace their damage.

However, Rextroy finds a level 60 enemy he can kill, an abomination in Eastern Plaguelands, which he pulls using a bug that casts Echoes of Lordaeron, an anti-undead damage boost given to whichever faction controls the most towers in the zone, on enemies when he resurrects.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

And sure, it takes 20 minutes. And sure, he can only kill it because the abomination has almost zero surprises, extra attacks, or abilities to stun him. But he still does it, getting a whopping… uh, 468 experience points for his trouble.

Perhaps the more game-breaking result of this build, then, is the fact that he can use it to out-pace fatigue damage, which generally stops players from swimming way out into the ocean. This lets him access a non-instanced version of the Drowned City dungeon, which is visible off the coast of Stranglethorn but cannot be visited outside of the dungeon without sleeping with the fishes.

While I think the extent of this build is probably something that'll get adjusted or patched out, I do sort of hope the spirit of it is kept the same—part of the promise of Forever was that weird item combinations or cool builds would emerge out of the woodwork and let folks do niche, but powerful things.

Perhaps it's not great that Rextroy can both tank and heal a dungeon with this setup at the same time, but I'd still like it to work in some capacity.

#3795. Will a Grand Theft Auto game ever be set outside of America? Rockstar offers a small glimmer of hope

The Grand Theft Auto games have always been synonymous with America; Americana is baked into the crime series' very being. Across its history, there's only ever been one GTA game set outside America: the London-based expansion of the original game.

GTA 6 follows this template, parodying the American state of Florida and the city of Miami. But what about the next game - will the series always be in America? Not necessarily.

In an interview with The Guardian, Rockstar North co-studio boss Rob Nelson propped the proverbial door open a sliver by saying: "Never say never." He then quickly followed that comment with: "But there’s still so much to do in America".

This is a topic Rockstar has responded to before, most notably when company co-founder and long-time GTA writer Dan Houser - who's no longer at Rockstar - discussed why the series always seemed to return to America. He said it was because cities like Miami and New York and Los Angeles are places where extreme juxtapositions exist. They're places where extreme wealth rubs shoulders with extreme poverty, and where organised crime can be found.

There's also something America infamously has that few other countries do, and that's free availability of guns, which is such a core tenet of a GTA experience.

Nevertheless, Obbe Vermeij - a former technical director at Rockstar North - revealed last year that a GTA: Tokyo almost happened. However, it wasn't going to be made by Rockstar but rather an external team in Japan.

While discussing the subject, Vermeij referred to America as "basically the epicenter of Western culture". "Everybody knows the cities, even people who haven't been there," Vermeij said. "They have a mental image of the cities. I'm afraid we're stuck in this loop of about five American cities. Let's just get used to it."

GTA 6 is just days away from its 19th November release on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. Rockstar recently clarified the game runs at 30FPS across all platforms and confirmed that while it's available through Xbox Cloud Gaming, it cannot be streamed to PCs or non-Xbox devices.

#3794. "We've finally reached this milestone": Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer mod CyberMP kicks off open beta after around six years preparing for cybermayhem

"Let's see how the project handles real player traffic"

After a couple of years of regular testing behind closed doors, Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer mod CyberMP is now out in open beta, giving anyone who fancies a bit of multi-merc action a chance to give it a go. Though, if you do, be prepared for bugs and crashes, as work on the mod is far from over with the release of this "true beta".

As shown off in the video above, CyberMP's not about being able to play through the base game's missions with friends, but rather cruise around Night City as a gang getting into races and PvP shootouts. In that regard, it seems more akin to GTA 4's online mode than GTA 5's, with classic improvised hijinks the main draw over being able to pull off gigs with a crew. Though, there do also look to be roleplaying servers which could scratch the itch of those more interested in pretending to be a merc than blowing up other people's rides.

"After almost six years of development, countless reworks, and code rewrites, we're finally launching the public beta," the modders wrote on Discord. "Anyone can jump in and play now — no invites or applications needed. Fair warning: this is a true beta. Crashes, desyncs, and server drops under heavy load are completely normal for now. That's exactly why we need testers. We welcome everyone: regular players, future server admins, and those who just love breaking game mechanics."

"Right now, our absolute priority is stability and fixing crashes," they continued later in the post. "New features are planned, but we need to polish the foundation first. A huge thank you to everyone who has been with us since the early versions, helped with closed testing, and patiently waited. We've finally reached this milestone. Let's see how the project handles real player traffic!"

According to the modders, CyberMP's "client doesn't have a digital signature yet", which could cause antivirus software not to be a fan of it. They're also anticipating "problems with the anti‑cheat system", so it may be worth holding off on giving the mod a go if you're not keen on being trolled by someone with the sort of destructive power usually reserved for megacorps and AIs from beyond the blackwall in the Cyberpunkverse.

For info on how to get CyberMP up and running, as well as create a custom server dedicated to the likes of roleplay or races, head over to its website. As you might expect, the mod requires a legit copy of Cyberpunk bought on either Steam, GOG, or the Epic store.

Colorful backdrops meet colorful characters in this solid-enough sixth entry into the series. The recasting of familiar characters is – largely – spot on

Joseph Zada makes for a credible Haymitch

The costumes and design are brilliantly barmy

Fiennes' pained Snow never quite convinces

Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy.

Like any franchise worth its salt, the past is always there to be mined. Back in 2023, The Hunger Games franchise relaunched with sturdy prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, set 64 years before we first meet Jennifer Lawrence's archer extraordinaire Katniss Everdeen. Now comes Sunrise on the Reaping, building on its predecessor with another look into the dim and distant. Set around the 50th Hunger Games, it's a chance to tell the origin story of Haymitch Abernathy.

Played in the originals by Woody Harrelson, who brought real soul to this role, this time it's the turn of Joseph Zada, the young, blonde-haired Australian recently seen opposite Florence Pugh in Netflix's East of Eden. With the script adapted from Suzanne Collins' 2025 novel, the fifth in the best-selling YA series, Zada's Haymitch is just 16 years old – twenty-four years before he becomes mentor to Katniss. But it's during this life-changing Games that he lights the fuse of his revolutionary spirit.

Directed by series regular Francis Lawrence, and scripted by Michael Lesslie and Billy Ray (who returns to the franchise for the first time since penning 2012's The Hunger Games), we're back in everyone's favourite dour-looking dystopia, Panem. Again hosting its annual adolescent deathmatch, this being the 50th of these deadly Games, it's time for something special. Every 25 editions, the so-called Quarter Quell comes into play, with a twist to the rules.

This time, each district must send double the number of tributes – two boys, two girls – to participate in the Capitol's bloody televised spectacle. During District 12's 'reaping', overseen by outlandishly attired Capitol escort Drusilla Sickle (Glenn Close), Haymitch avoids being picked – until he intervenes when one of the tributes fatally makes a dash for it. One of the chosen four, he's joined by his childhood friend Louella (Molly McCann) and two others – Wyatt (Ben Wang) and Maysilee (Mckenna Grace).

Release date: November 20 (US), November 18 (UK) Available: In theatersDirector: Francis LawrenceRuntime: 2h 38m

While Wyatt is an oddsmaker, known for calculating survival and betting odds, Maysilee is the original owner of the Mockingjay pin that became Katniss' symbol of rebellion. But here, the rebellion is all Haymitch's, as his hatred for Panem's totalitarian rule begins to swell. "It's not living – it's surviving," he says of the world he now lives in, his desire to bring down the Hunger Games fuelling his journey to the Capitol.

It means leaving his girl behind, Lenore Dove (Whitney Peak) – cue some moist-eyed moments that fail to move – and making some alliances. Among them, Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons), long before he became a leader of the rebel movement in the Districts. Here, he's a cameraman assigned to capture the 'reaping', telling Haymitch "presentation is everything" when he forces him and Lenore to re-enact their tear-strewn goodbye for the cameras.

One of the real pleasures of Sunrise on the Reaping is seeing how Lawrence has recast some of the key characters from the original quartet of films. Dressed in lairy gold braid, Kieran Culkin is a delight as the Games' verbose host Caesar Flickerman, previously embodied by Stanley Tucci. The same goes for Elle Fanning as the daffy, purple-haired stylist Effie Trinket, who brings even more quirk than Elizabeth Banks managed.

It's Plemons, though, who truly purrs as Plutarch, effortlessly capturing the character's slippery nature. Certainly, he feels like perfect casting, given he's something of a spiritual successor to the late Philip Seymour Hoffman, who played Heavensbee in the originals. Close, complete with orange fright wig, is similarly having a ball as Drusilla, leaving only Ralph Fiennes' President Coriolanus Snow as an example of recasting that doesn't quite gel, lacking the sheer menace that Donald Sutherland brought to the role.

Sunrise on the Reaping works as both a standalone and a satisfying part of a bigger whole

Running at an indulgent 158 minutes, Sunrise on the Reaping does lack tension somewhat, suffering from the same join-the-dots curse that afflicts many prequels. We know the outcome already – in this case, that Haymitch survives and goes on to meet Katniss. It's this that rather lets the air out of the film, and even Lawrence's energetic direction and Zada's puppyish enthusiasm can't do much to steer that last act to an emotional crescendo.

Sometimes the script seems a little too desperate to sew up those connections to the earlier films. Naturally, there are further references to Katniss – including in a slightly ill-judged coda that adds little to the story. But for the most part, Sunrise on the Reaping works as both a standalone and a satisfying part of a bigger whole. With glorious costumes by Bina Daigeler and lavish production design by Uli Hanisch, it's a feast to watch, even if it never quite hits the highs of its predecessors.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping releases on November 20, with previews from November 18. For more, here are the most exciting upcoming movies still coming your way in 2026, and beyond.

#3792. Paradox boss Frederik Wester stepping down after several tumultuous years for the Cities Skylines and Stellaris publisher

Deputy CEO Mattias Lilja taking over role.

Paradox Interactive's Frederik Wester has announced he's stepping down from the role of CEO after a combined decade and a half leading the company. The news follows several tumultuous years for the publisher best known for grand strategy games including Stellaris, Europa Universalis, and Crusader Kings 3.

In a statement announcing the change in leadership, Paradox said Wester had "decided to step down as CEO to continue focusing on the company's long-term development as a member of the Board." Paradox's current deputy CEO, Mattias Lilja, will take over Wester's role from 4th January 2027. Wester is to remain in the position until then in order "to ensure an orderly transition".

"I'm truly grateful to all our engaged players and talented colleagues who contribute to outstanding gaming experiences every day," Wester said of his decision. "They are the ones who made these years amazing. My plan was never to be CEO for life. The goal was to build the foundation before passing the baton on for the next chapter in the company's journey. Since I returned as CEO, we've streamlined our strategy, rebuilt our pipeline and developed our commercial offering. Mattias has had a central role in laying this foundation, and now is the right time to hand over. Given his experience and vision, he is exceptionally well positioned to take the company to its next level."

Wester has twice served as Paradox CEO since joining the company in 2003. His first stint ran from 2009 to 2018, after which he became Paradox's executive chairman of the board. He returned to the CEO role in 2021, and has overseen a troubled period for the company. This has included the embattled development of Vampire: The Masquerade Bloodlines 2 - which finally launched last October after multiple delays, near cancellation, and a switch in developer. Unfortunately the game failed to resonate with critics and audiences, and Paradox announced a 162 percent decline in operating profit earlier this year as a result of its commercial failure.

Wester's most recent watch - which began with an admittance of "inappropriate behaviour" amid a damning report into Paradox's workplace culture - has also seen the high-profile cancellation of Sims competitor Life By You, an indefinite delay for Prison Architect 2 after Paradox parted ways with original developer Double Eleven, and a split with BattleTech studio Harebrained Schemes following the commercial failure of The Lamplighters League. Paradox's Cities Skylines 2 has also been blighted with controversy: after a disastrous launch in 2023, its console release is still yet to emerge, and development is now being handled by a new studio after Paradox split with former developer Colossal Order last year. In 2004, Wester admitted the publisher had "made the wrong calls in several projects".

Despite all this, incoming CEO Mattias Lilja remains buoyant. "Paradox has a unique DNA that has made us one of the greats in deep and engaging strategy and management games," he wrote in a statement announcing his promotion. "Now we’re stepping up the pace: we will make further investments in our core business, push the boundaries of our game design, work even more closely with our loyal players, develop more and better tools and services that benefit both modders and players, and continue to sharpen our ways of working and our organisation, with player value in focus."

Paradox, does of course, have some promising games on its upcoming slate. Alongside continued work on grand strategy stalwarts like Crusader Kings 3, Europa Universalis 5, and Stellaris, next year sees the release of Lego Skylines, and post-apocalyptic grand strategy game Afterworld is also on the way.

#3791. "Nobody was hurt" in shooting near Clockwork Revolution devs InXile Entertainment's office, the Xbox-owned studio and police confirm

"Nobody was hurt" in a shooting last week near the California office of Clockwork Revolution developers InXile, both the studio and local police have confirmed. The incident, which took place on November 11th, is currently being investigated and police have reportedly taken a suspect into custody.

"Officers got there [on November 11th]," Tustin police sergeant Christopher Peterson said in statement to Aftermath. "They responded to a report of a drive-by shooting there. Located multiple shell casings. Nobody was hurt. Processed the crime scene, and then sometime [Friday] morning, a little before 11 [AM], they took a suspect into custody. And the investigation is still kind of ongoing as to where and why."

"We’re relieved that no one was hurt at our inXile office," a spokesperson for InXile said in a separate statement. "Our focus is on supporting our team, and we are working closely with law enforcement as they investigate."

InXile are set to release steampunk RPG Clockwork Revolution next year. The studio, developers of the likes of Wasteland 3 and The Bard's Tale IV, are one of the few Xbox-owned studios not to have been affected - at least as of writing - by Microsoft's ongoing mass layoffs this year.

Since being announced in 2023, Clockwork Revolution's dripped with Bioshock-ish vibes and popped up semi-regularly at Xbox showcases. "Wield the power of an incredible device to travel back in time, changing the past and rewriting the future of the city you call home: the vibrant steampunk metropolis of Avalon," reads its Steam synopsis. "In this immersive RPG, you'll step into the shoes of Morgan Vanette, a fully customizable player-character and member of the Rotten Row Hooligans. Travel between past and present as you battle the ruthless Lady Ironwood, who has been manipulating time to keep the working class struggling while amassing immense wealth and power."

Best wishes to the staff at InXile, here's hoping that going forwards they're able to get with making what's looking to be an intriguingly funky game without enduring any more concerning incidents like this one.

Final Fantasy 14 is set to make some big changes when the upcoming expansion Evercold releases in February. An overhaul to combat, dailies, and new raid difficulties are set to shake things up and, hopefully, keep people sticking around for longer.

And judging by a recent Letter from the Producer, Naoki Yoshida really wants folks coming back to see what Evercold is all about. So much so that the game's offering 30 free days for long-gone adventurers… or a quick-and-dirty paid skip if you're so inclined.

"Encouraging players to return is no mean feat," Yoshida wrote. "People pause their adventures for all kinds of reasons, including dissatisfaction and loss of interest. Although we continually update the game to address such issues, the fact remains that getting players to resume their journey is a difficult task indeed."

I can only assume that for that reason, the decision's been made to offer up a $9 cash shop item that'll skip you through Endwalker's patch story, as well as all of Dawntrail up until the final story patch. Now Final Fantasy 14 has offered paid story skips in the past—it still does—but this is the first time it's explicitly offered one for the current expansion. Usually the skips'll stop dead before the current expansion, meaning you still need to play through the newest story.

It's a pretty niche paid skip, too. You'll need to have at least completed Endwalker's main story and have a level 90 job on your chosen character, and even then you'll still have to level up to 100 in your own time in order to tackle the final patch quest of Dawntrail. But worry not, if you haven't played the game in six months, you'll be able to snap up 30 days of free game time until January 14. Plenty of time to get a job to max level and prepare for Evercold.

I'm mostly surprised by the introduction of this paid item because Yoshida has long been rather protective of the game's story. Something he admits in this very same letter: "I strongly believe that FF14 is a story-driven MMORPG," he wrote. "On top of that, skipping it all means you likely won't be familiar with the battle system and therefore will become a burden for other players in multiplayer content."

I do find it a little funny that Yoshida is worried that story skippers will weigh others down in dungeons and the like—I've played many a level 100 dungeon with folks who have clearly played enough to understand how to play yet still can't press their buttons properly.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

But anyway, Yoshida does admit that there is a lot of story to get through. "The Hydaelyn and Zodiark saga alone encompasses five expansions' worth of content," he wrote. "And with Dawntrail marking the start of the second saga, plus the coming addition of Evercold, the story continues to unfold into something even larger."

It really does feel like Square Enix wants Evercold to mark a big resurgence for the game, one I really do hope pays off for the developer. I've been playing off-and-on since A Realm Reborn and have seen just about every evolution the game has taken, and also the ways it has stagnated over time. Its confidence in trying to draw people back has me excited for the changes that are coming.

#3789. After two weeks of multiplayer downtime, Dark Souls 2 & 3's mysterious server "issue" has been fixed, so it no longer feels so lonely online

Developer FromSoftware has announced that online multiplayer servers for Dark Souls 2 and 3 are back online following a nearly two-week outage.

FromSoftware temporarily disabled multiplayer on 30th October, citing what it called "a server issue". Some speculated this could be related to the recently discovered PHP security bug, which impacted a number of other games.

FromSoftware never specified the exact issue impacting its servers, and today's statement is equally vague. "Regarding the temporary suspension of the game server for Dark Souls 2, and Dark Souls 3, the investigation has been completed and the fix has been applied. The game server and online features are now restored," a notice on Dark Souls' official site reads.

"We sincerely apologise for the inconvenience caused, and thank you for your patience and understanding."

Online servers do more in FromSoftware games than simply facilitating co-op and PvP; they're also responsible for handling messages players leave for each other in-game, as well as the ghostly representations of players who just went through the same area, helping the Dark Souls series' forlorn worlds feel a little less solitary.

This isn't the first time Dark Souls servers have gone offline, either. In 2022, servers for all three games went offline due to a vulnerability that allowed malicious code to run on them. In that instance, it took FromSoftware three months to bring servers back online for some games, and as many as nine months for others.

In other FromSoftware news, the studio recently announced - following months of speculation - it's officially delaying the Switch 2-exclusive The Duskbloods to sometime in 2027.

Game of Thrones showrunners David Benioff and D.B. Weiss created the show with Alexander Woo. Speaking to Netflix's Tudum, the co-creators explained what viewers can expect from the returning show.

"The tone really changes once you get to the second season," they said. "It's much bigger. Things get wilder, the conflicts get more cosmic. Once people see it on the screen, they’re going to understand why we've been so excited for this season, in particular."

#3786. The Witcher 3 uses gen-AI to enhance Geralt's Polish voice following actor's stroke - "I do think this is one of those ways where you can use AI ethically"

"I have great trust ... for the creators of this game."

CD Projekt Red has revealed that it used - and is using - generative AI technology to treat and alter the voice of the Polish actor who portrayed Geralt of Rivia in upcoming Witcher 3 expansion Songs of the Past.

The actor, Jacek Rozenek, has portrayed Geralt of Rivia in all the major Witcher games, meaning his voice has become as synonymous with the role in Poland as Doug Cockle's has for people playing in English. But Rozenek suffered a severe stroke in 2019 that left him temporarily unable to speak, and when he was able to talk and perform again, the tonality and quality of his voice had changed.

It's for these reasons that CD Projekt Red - with Rozenek's consent - employed the help of a company called Respeecher to alter the lines he recorded for The Witcher 3's Songs of the Past expansion using generative-AI technology. As confirmed to Game File, an AI trained on Rozenek's previous Witcher work is retreating his recordings to make them sound more like the Geralt you hear elsewhere in The Witcher 3.

"The point is that this voice should be as close as possible to my voice from 12 years ago," Jacek Rozenek explained. "I have great trust ... for the creators of this game."

Game File heard both treated and untreated recordings of Rozenek's Songs of the Past work, and reported a "significant" difference between them. Rozenek's untreated voice was apparently "deep and gravelly" and "noticeably rougher than his recordings for the original game". But treated, the voice was "far smoother and sounds younger", and closer to the original Witcher 3 Geralt recordings.

This isn't the first time CD Projekt Red has used generative AI for voice recordings in one of its games. The studio worked with Respeecher in 2023 to produce new voiceover lines for Cyberpunk 2077 expansion Phantom Liberty. Viktor Vektor actor Miłogost "Miłek" Reczek passed away in 2021, after the original game was released, and CD Projekt Red didn't want to recast the role. Reczek's sons apparently gave their blessing for their father's voice to be artificially generated.

"I do think this is one of those ways where you can use AI ethically with consent and also to do something good," CD Projekt Red localisation producer Mikołaj Szwed told Game File, referring to the Rozenek recordings.

"For future projects, when we consider Geralt is becoming older and has a deeper voice, this is not a problem for us at all. It's more about this specific situation here, where we have both the voice from 12 years ago and from now next to each other, which could kind of take people out of the experience and feel that there is this difference."

The third Witcher 3 expansion, Songs of the Past, releases at some point next year, an unprecedented 12 years after the original game launched. It adds an entirely new region, Letten, and centres its main story around Geralt's missing bardic bestie Dandelion, whose family lives there.

In preparation for the expansion, a remastered version of The Witcher 3 was released a couple of months ago, overhauling the old role-playing adventure and bringing its baseline presentation more in line with what we'd expect from a modern game; it also overhauled some animations and enemy behaviours and reworked skill trees. For that reason, old-gen consoles PS4 and Xbox One won't receive the Songs of the Past expansion, despite The Witcher 3 being available on them.

As Sydney Sweeney continues to generate buzz due to her acting career, buzzy lingerie line, those splashy ads and more business ventures, there’s been a continued focus on her personal life. That includes her relationship with Scooter Braun, who has reportedly been helping her make career decisions. As rumors continue to swirl around their relationship, it’s been alleged that Sweeney wants to move to the UK. Now, there’s apparently more evidence that she’s planning a move like Meghan Markle and Prince Harry’s.

Not only has it been alleged that the Euphoria alum is looking for a new residence in the UK, and this claim has sparked a bit of speculation. A recent report from The Sun sheds more light on the purported matter and, according to the outlet, Sweeney recently viewed a property in the village of Little Tew. Per a source, the actress has allegedly informed her people in her inner circle that she’s aiming to split her time between the UK and her multiple properties in the United States. A source for the tabloid also said this:

Sydney has ­visited the Cotswolds twice in the past ten months, and absolutely loves it. She viewed property there within the past three months.

If Sweeney were to make the move, she would actually become just another one of the famous people who live in the area. Among the celebrities who live in the area are David and Victoria Beckham, Ellen DeGeneres and her wife, Portia de Rossi (whose house was thought to have flooded in 2024) and Jeremy Clarkson. The Sun’s insider went on to allege that due to the presence of multiple stars, Sweeney wouldn’t have to worry about residents making a fuss over her, and there’s apparently another benefit:

She doesn’t get bothered by locals, who are all well-used to seeing A-listers, and finds village life incredibly cute and quaint. It’s also a huge change of pace from LA and all the vultures circling. And she can lead a more peaceful life in the countryside. Pinewood Studios are also only about an hour away, meaning she could easily stay at home while filming should she land the gig.

This should all be taken with a grain of salt, considering that no one from Sydney Sweeney’s camp has confirmed or denied that she’s planning to make a new home across the pond. Still, this news comes at an interesting time, considering what’s been going on with the Duke and Duchess of Sussex as of late.

It was reported this past August that Markle and Prince Harry were moving back to the UK alongside their two kids, Archie and Lilibet. For the past six years, the pair lived in Montecito, California, as they relocated to the state after stepping back from roles as senior members of the British Royal Family. Harry and Markle reportedly used a private jet to return to the UK, and the trip allegedly cost them $120,000 in total.

Since returning to the country, the Duke and Duchess’ family has reportedly stayed with friends in the aforementioned Cotswolds. Earlier this month, though, it was reported that the pair had already slightly relocated. Apparently Markle, Harry and their brood moved to the “main house” on the estate after having lived in a “property on the estate.” As for the couple’s attempts to find a place of their own, it’s been alleged that their search has been stalled due to their “champagne tastes” purportedly not matching their financial portfolio.

The public at large will just have to wait and see whether the Duke and Duchess manage to land on a new property in the Cotswolds or somewhere else in the UK. In the meantime, those interested in updates on Sydney Sweeney may continue to watch for any further evidence of a reported move.

A mini PC with Intel's G3 chip would rock, but alas, we're left with just four Xe3 cores instead.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Motherboard manufacturer Biostar has just announced the BIPTL-IHT, a mini motherboard complete with an integrated Panther Lake-H processor. It's the first desktop Panther Lake motherboard to be released in retail.

As spotted by VideoCardz, the motherboard range has support for up to 128 GB of DDR-7200 MHz SO-DIMM memory and can come with the following chips:

All of these chips come with Xe3 graphics with four Xe cores, and are lacking the punchy integrated B390 iGPU (and its 12 Xe3 cores) that some mobile Panther Lake chips have. You can still do some light gaming on these integrated graphics, but you won't be making yourself a mini gaming PC with Biostar's latest.

Instead, it seems like the purpose of this motherboard is to support industrial PCs, but given Xe3 graphics support hardware-accelerated AV1 encoding and decoding, one could feasibly use the motherboard in a mini media server PC instead.

You are getting two M.2 Key-M slots here, with PCIe 5.0 x4 and PCIe 4.0 x2 connections. This allows for NVMe storage, and the memory is dual-channel too. You also get two HDMI ports, two DisplayPort 1.4 ports, and the motherboard can support up to four displays at once.

As it's a 'Thin' Mini-ITX motherboard, its dimensions are 170 mm by 170 mm. That's very small. We don't yet have a release date or price point for this motherboard range.

Still, it's a bit of a shame we don't have any mini motherboards with gaming-worthy integrated Panther Lake mobile chips yet. Especially as GPU prices are so high. I managed to get the chance to test out the Intel G3 Extreme in the Acer Predator Atlas 8 handheld, and it's pretty incredible for a chip with integrated graphics. It rocks both gaming and productivity tasks, given the size and heat.

#3783. GTA 6 hacker pleads guilty to 2022 Rockstar Games breach which the company claim cost them $5 million

Hacker was previously sentenced to stay in a secure hospital

A hacker has pleaded guilty to a number of online crimes, including the 2022 breach of Rockstar Games which resulted in a bunch of mid-development clips of GTA 6 in action leaking onto the net.

The BBC report that, on November 16th, Arion Kurtaj pleaded guilty at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar Games hack and a number of others he carried out with the hacking gang Lapsus$ while aged 16 and 17. Kurtaj, now aged 21, was previously sentenced to stay in a secure hospital indefinitely due to the severity of his autism, but was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial. He'll be sentenced at a later date.

Kurtaj carried out the 2022 Rockstar hack while on bail for other hacking offences and being housed at a Travelodge hotel under police protection, the latter on account of rival hackers threatening to attack him over stolen Bitcoin stashes. The Rockstar hack was reportedly done using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into the hotel room's TV, plus a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.

90 clips of unfinished GTA 6 were flung online by that hack, with Rockstar having refused to cooperate with Kurtaj's demand via an internal Slack channel that the company contact him on massaging app Telegram within 24 hours. Rockstar claimed the breach cost them $5m million to recover from, in addition to staff having to waste thousands of hours.

Earlier this year, GTA 6 suffered yet another leak, with a hacker or hackers going by "Cyberleek" posting various videos of the game in action. Rockstar and parent company Take-Two quickly sprung into action, taking down videos, filing subpoenas, and issuing a statement that called the leak "heartbreaking".

Hopefully with the game's console release later this week, those will be the only two GTA 6 leaks which have to be added to the annals of gaming history. As much as marketing can leave a bad taste in the mouth, especially when it barely shows anything of the actual product being advertised, neither of the GTA 6 leaks served much of a purpose beyond forcing people to waste some time and energy talking about the perpetrators.

The Ice Arrows in the OoT remake are the final reward of the Gerudo Training Grounds

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Ice Arrows in OoT Remake are an optional upgrade that allows you to fire freezing projectiles that hold enemies in place, but while you might expect to find them in a frozen or watery area, they're paradoxically kept in a desert building in the late game of Ocarina of Time, the final reward for completing the Gerudo Training Grounds. Below I'll lay out the exact location of the Ice Arrows and how you can get them from the Grounds themselves, as well as what you'll need to complete it effectively.

To get the Ice Arrows, players need to go to the Gerudo Training Grounds, an optional building that only becomes accessible after you complete the Gerudo Fortress as part of the main story, once Link becomes an adult.

It's found on the path South of the Fortress, at the location on the map shown above. However, to get inside will cost you 30 Rupees, paid to the Gerudo Guard on the door. If you leave later and come back, you'll need another 30 Rupees, so it's best to do it in a single go if possible.

The Gerudo Training Grounds are a series of dungeon rooms arranged in a circle around a single treasure room filled with locked doors. The doors have to be got through to reach the Ice Arrows in the middle, meaning you need to find eight Small Keys around the Training Grounds.

Each room has a Small Key somewhere inside, and will offer its own challenges. It might be a puzzle, a gauntlet of enemies, or a mixture of the two.

To complete all the puzzles, you'll need to make sure you have the following items and unlocks, as the Training Grounds can't be completed without them:

If you don't have all of these, you won't be able to complete the Training Grounds and will have to come back later, repaying the 30 Rupee entry fee to get in. I also recommend you bring a good supply of arrows, bombs, and potions to ensure that you don't struggle in combat encounters or are killed by traps.

#3781. After days of controversy, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned

Nvidia's founder and CEO Jensen Huang has resigned from his position as leader of one of the most valuable companies in the world.

After days mired in controversy, which began amid reports of Huang's alleged affair with a Chinese spy, Nvidia has announced Huang's resignation as company president, chief executive officer, and board member, effective immediately. Finance chief Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO and will remain in the position until a permanent CEO is chosen.

"Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position," Harvey Jones, chair of Nvidia's board of directors wrote in a statement accompanying the news. "She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing Nvidia's strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption."

Kress, in the same announcement, says she intends to build on the foundation laid by Huang over the past 33 years, and "continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead." Perhaps unsurprisingly, there's no mention of gaming graphics cards in there.

Nvidia's announcement ends by thanking Huang for his time at the company: "Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry."

Nvidia's board met on Wednesday to decide whether to remove Huang amid allegations he had participated in a second affair, this time with a subordinate, following reports of his alleged affair with a Chinese spy. That initial incident prompted a company-wide apology from Huang and an independent investigation exploring whether he'd been the target of a "foreign intelligence effort".

Nvidia will likely remain under increased scrutiny moving forward. There are particular concerns around the company's chips being imported to China despite trade bans.

#3780. Intel are being sued for "misleading" investors about "a massive glut of unwanted PC inventory" thanks to AI-fuelled price hikes

Tech giant Intel are being taken to court for allegedly "misleading" their investors about the sheer scale of the impact of generative AI-fuelled component price hikes on PC sales. The class action lawsuit in question claims that Intel's distribution and manufacturing partners have had to deal with "a massive glut of unwanted PC inventory", and that the gains from Intel's investments in AI datacenters aren't enough to make up for slowing sales of PCs to regular Josephines who just want fancy boxes they can play Deadlock on.

All this follows Intel's last round of quarterly results, in which they announced a significant revenue fall; this triggered an Intel stock price drop from $92.07 per share on October 29th to $65.76 per share the next day, which this week's lawsuit characterises as "the largest single-day price decline for Intel common stock in over 50 years".

The lawyers in question are from Robbins LLP, who specialise in "shareholder, whistleblower, antitrust, & consumer litigation". In a press release, they say they've filed suit on behalf of anybody who bought Intel stock from July 23rd to October 29th this year.

The suit claims that Intel neglected to tell investors that falling PC and component sales were having a "materially greater negative impact" on their third financial quarter 2026 Client Computing and Physical AI Groupresults than Intel had previously stated – to the tune of "hundreds of millions of dollars" in revenue shrinkage, compared to the previous quarter, with the situation still expected to "worsen".

They also accuse the company of keeping schtum about the aforesaid "massive glut of unwanted PC inventory", together with the fact that "any positive impacts to Intel’s business and financial results resulting from data center construction and other aspects of the AI boom were more than offset by the negative effects on the Company’s business and financial results resulting from the PC market slowdown and the excess inventory buildup described above."

Finally, they say Intel bosses have failed to disclose that they're struggling to procure an adequate supply of substrates – that is, materials used to create the base layer of chips, circuit boards and similar components. As such, the lawyers claim, Intel couldn't "ramp up production to meet data center CPU demand even if the Company chose to divert production resources because of a slowdown in PC-related sales."

Once the Godzilla of personal computing, Intel haven't been having a brilliant few years. Back in 2024, they recorded a multi-billion dollar quarterly loss, pushing then-CEO Pat Gelsinger to resign. As regards sales of gaming PCs, they've fallen behind AMD, though they've reportedly taken some ground back recently as regards desktop CPUs. As regards graphics cards, they have long been dwarfed by Nvidia.

Any Intel investor who wants a piece of that lawsuit has until January 12th 2027 to sign up as a lead plaintiff – that is, a court appointee who represents the interests of other class members. As regards us little people who don't buy stock in huge technology corporations, all this merely continues the weird existential crisis wrought upon 'traditional' gaming and computing hardware by the feckless quest to sell a better chatbot.

Call of Duty is an inherently conservative series. You know what you're getting: guns, explosions, cinematic flourishes inspired by action movies, and probably some jingoism. And that's largely what the annual series' adherents seem to want. But it could be so much more.

Taylor Kurosaki, writer and co-director for Call of Duty: Infinite Warfare, tells us he still thinks it has broad potential. That's why Infinite Warfare was set in the future—though, at the time, the team didn't realise it would end up being the third futuristic CoD, following Advanced Warfare and Black Ops 3.

"Look, Call of Duty is a massive tree with a lot of branches, right? It can be World War 2. The team at IW had prototyped a medieval Call of Duty. Where you were a knight and had a sword and all kinds of crazy shit. But if it's a war story, sure, it can be Call of Duty."

I would love for that to be true. Call of Duty: The American Revolutionary War, Call of Duty: The Hundred Years War, Call of Duty: Napoleon. A military romp that isn't set between 1941 and 2065. After 23 years, it would be nice to see it spread out a bit.

But big swings are not in CoD's nature. Or rather, Activision isn't particularly interested in rocking the money boat. A medieval CoD isn't the only massive detour the series almost took. Before it was forced to salvage Infinity Ward's Modern Warfare 3, Sledgehammer was working on a third-person horror game set in Vietnam, called Call of Duty: Fog of War.

"We wanted to make a scary version of Vietnam," Sledgehammer co-founder Glen Schofield told us last year. "And not just scary, we wanted intense battles that were personal, but stuff you've never seen before. We were making it, and we were really psyched about having you go through tunnels, and everything is scary because there's not much light down there. Sometimes you're shooting in the dark."

When Vince Zampella and Jason West left Infinity Ward amid a legal dispute, Activision told Sledgehammer to drop their project and pivot to Modern Warfare 3. It was never allowed to return to Fog of War.

#3778. As low-effort AI slop continues to flood Steam, yet more developers announce game delays caused by Valve's growing approval backlog

"There's no outcome of this that allows Valve neutrality on AI".

More indie developers say they've been forced to delay the impending release of their games as a result of Steam's growing approvals backlog - a relatively recent problem that's believed to stem from an influx of AI slop on the platform.

Earlier this month, developers began complaining about delays to Valve's approval process, which was extending the time it took to get their games published on Steam. Valve responded, explaining approval times could now take up to 12 days, due to the number of submissions it was having to re-review. One week on, the situation doesn't seem to have improved.

New turn-based tower defence game Australia Did It: End-of-the-World Railway Defense Business, co-developed by acclaimed indie designer Rami Ismail and Aesthetician Labs, was previously set for release on 10th November. Unfortunately, the game has now been delayed while the wait continues for Valve to review the latest build.

"We're still waiting for Steam to give us the final greenlight and finish their build review process," publisher Mystic Forge wrote on the Steam forums. "We have been stuck waiting for it for a few weeks now and unfortunately we just don't know when they will get around to reviewing it at this point."

Speaking to Eurogamer, Ismail added that Australia Did It has been in Steam's approval queue for much longer than he's used to: "We've been in the queue since 20th October, failed over a minor controller input issue on 5th November (which we resolved the same day), and we've been waiting again since with no meaningful response from Valve despite follow-ups."

"I'm used to hold-and-wait patterns on console," Ismail continued, "but Steam has historically been much more snappy - 10-14 days pre-launch was usually enough to fail twice and still ship on time," he added.

Amazing Slot Survivor (A.S.S.), the debut title from TwoMenGames, is facing similar issues, and has had to retract its release date announcement after being stuck in Steam's approval queue. Amazing Slot Survivor, which adds a slot machine spin to the bullet heaven auto-shooting genre, was initially set for release on 13th November.

"Steam's review process for the release is taking longer than we expected," TwoMenGames wrote in a message on Steam. "We know many of you have been counting on the schedule we announced earlier, and we are very sorry to bring you this [postponement] news instead of the good news you were hoping for." Amazing Slot Survivor's demo, which was previously set to disappear with the game's full release, has returned to Steam until the developer announces a new launch date.

These are far from the only examples, and a cursory look on social media reveals many more indie games are affected by the problem, including the likes of Bottled by Bears, and Food Devils.

Valve recently attempted to address the delays its facing by introducing stricter submission guidelines designed to stop the lowest-effort games, such as those vibe-coded entirely with gen-AI, from joining its approval queue. However, Ismail doesn't think that's good enough.

"I am concerned that Valve trying to avoid taking a political position on AI is forcing them into choices that will inevitably be worse for developers," he told Eurogamer. "If sloppers can submit several game clones a day through automated systems, the only way for Valve to stem the tide of games damaging genuine developers' work is to put constraints on game distribution, increase fees, or make the process more complicated.

"In the 'open market' Valve seems to so adore, they're going to be the ones carrying the costs for moderation, so I don't think they'll like the open market on this - but there's no outcome of this that allows Valve neutrality on AI and not do things that will ultimately make life worse for genuine developers," he added.

#3777. Each new GTA moves the series closer and closer to the original Mafia, the open-world game that bettered Rockstar

This week sees the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, the open-world crime 'em up that's been in development for at least eight years and has been waited on by fans for even longer. Naturally, over on PC we're still waiting for a port to be announced, let alone a release date to circle in our calendars. But, as happens whenever a new GTA is on the horizon, I think about Mafia: City of Lost Heaven.

Released less than a year after Grand Theft Auto 3, Mafia is perhaps a more prescient example of Rockstar's future than their own.

Set in Lost Heaven, a shoe-in for 1930s Chicago, Illinois, you play through Tommy Angelo's rise from a taxi driver, who has a chance run in with the Salieri crime family, to one of the gang's main enforcers in their fight against their rivals, the Morellos.

The influences on developers Illusion Softworks are obviously cinematic, with whole sequences ripped from The Godfather films and Goodfellas (and I'd argue there's a sprinkling of Once Upon A Time In America for good measure). A habit they share with Rockstar, who also pull liberally from crime films that share the settings of their games. But Illusion Softworks are also clearly interested in capturing the history of the Prohibition era, too. The story begins in the aftermath of the 1929 Wall Street Crash and the depression that followed, running through until the late 30s, and you see that time pass in the city around you. Buildings that are under construction at the start of the game are completed by its end, a used car lot in Chinatown sits empty for most of the game until business picks up with the economy, but most enjoyable of all is that the cars driving the streets change. At first the roads are filled with Ford Model-T-inspired vehicles that basically look like horse carriages with engines, but by the end of the game they've all become much sleeker creatures that have left their early carriage influences behind.

The city Illusion Softworks built also has a dedication to verisimilitude that we see Rockstar adopting in their later games. As you drive Lost Heaven's streets, you must pay attention to speed limits and red lights, as speeding and running traffic lights will both earn you a fine if a policeman spots you. For fans of public transport, there are streetcars and overhead trams you can ride to navigate the city, too. Two other touches I love: when you reload your gun, you dump the whole clip instead of returning the unfired bullets to a magic ammo reservoir, and vehicles can run out of fuel if you drive them too far.

Much had been made of all the simulations running under the surface of Grand Theft Auto 6, such as fully realised cloud formation, a smell reaction system, and… fuel tanks that can run empty. No doubt they're significantly more impressive than what's on show in Mafia, and this isn't about putting the two games against each other (even if one of them was likely made for less than the other studio spent on coffee runs across its eight-year development). Nor is it about saying history recognised the wrong game: Grand Theft Auto 3 was a huge step forward in open-world gaming and Mafia was recognised and celebrated in its time. It's about something else.

Back in 2002, Illusion Softworks offered a different kind of open-world crime game. One that was more mature despite having a lower age rating. Grand Theft Auto was undoubtedly more influential, sparking imitators that mostly opted to follow its tone and sensibilities – Saints Row began in a similar place to GTA 3 and as the series continued leaned further into the silliness and parody, for instance. But while for many years Mafia stood as a sign to an open world path that could have been taken, the longer Grand Theft Auto series has gone on, the more Rockstar have found their way toward the example set by Illusion Softworks. The games are still aiming for bombastic comedy at times, but they're also interested in the likes of newly-arrived-in-America Niko Belic, or Michael de Santa, a retired criminal haunted by his past. They're much richer protagonists than Claude, the silent character you play in GTA 3.

The Mafia series has continued, marked by ideas that remain as interesting as what was on show in the original. In Mafia 3, you play Lincoln Clay, a black soldier returned from the war in Vietnam and brought into the family. Set in a take on New Orleans, Louisiana, during the civil rights movement, you face overt racism. Linger too long in white, wealthy neighbourhoods and the residents will call on the police to move you along. And the Definitive Edition remake of the first game, released in 2020, is a rare example of a game that both captures the spirit of the original and justifies its existence by expanding and bettering the story. Though I don't think any of its sequels have been as innovative, nor as forward thinking, as the first game.

I don't want to come across as Rockstar-bashing. The studio have continued to push the open-world genre forward with every release and I want to see what other developers lift from GTA 6 for their own games. But I'm even more pleased that as the studio's aged, their work has grown closer to Illusion Softworks'.

SPOILERS are ahead for Scrubs Season 2 through episode 8. Catch up with a Hulu subscription before reading ahead!

Ever since the Scrubs revival made its way onto the 2026 TV schedule, I’ve been tuning in, and it really hasn’t disappointed. Last season was good, but I think Season 2 has been especially stellar, and that has a lot to do with what subject matter is getting the spotlight. The new season reeled me in with Dr. Cox’s health developments, but now I’m really hooked thanks to what’s going on with J.D. and Elliot’s relationship. And, I think it’s time I discuss it.

When Scrubs returned to TV, I was instantly taken aback by the choice to make J.D. and Elliot exes. Bill Lawrence defended the decision to CinemaBlend months ago, saying that the couple just couldn’t go a few episodes without “being a horrible couple,” so he wanted to be realistic.

While it bummed me out at first, I’m starting to really appreciate the sort of nuanced conversations that come with J.D. and Elliot no longer being together. They’re both still co-workers and co-parents, so they have to make it work as friends, but I just don’t feel like I see enough relationships like this on TV. My own parents have been divorced for awhile, and I’ve watched their relationship evolve in a new way amidst still being my parents. I know it’s quite common, and yet, for many TV couples it’s either them being together or not.

On that topic, the episode from a couple of weeks ago, “My Story,” really threw me for a loop in the best way. In it, we’re led to believe that J.D. and Elliot end up going to dinner together and deciding to try to make things work again. We learned more about why things fell apart between them, too. But ultimately, we learn the whole scenario is happening in J.D.’s head, and he decides not to pursue their relationship in fear of hurting her once again.

I’m all for love, and a part of me wants to see these two back together, but I'm also really enjoying seeing this unique dynamic on Scrubs. There’s clearly a lot of real love between them, but they were also famously on-again-off again throughout the original run of Scrubs. It feels like we’re getting to watch these two attempt to heal in real time and decide how to go forward in their lives, between being busy medical professionals and being parents, too.

I guess for the time being I’m not thinking about whether I want them together ultimately or not, I just want to continue to see this difficult dynamic between them be explored. I think Scrubs is one of those few shows that can simultaneously be hilarious and emotional, and I think what’s going on between J.D. and Elliot is something worth stretching out for a while.

Sarah El-Mahmoud has been with CinemaBlend since 2018 after graduating from Cal State Fullerton with a degree in Journalism. Now she's into covering YA television and movies, and plenty of horror. Word webslinger. All her writing should be read in Sarah Connor’s Terminator 2 voice over.

#3775. World of Warcraft: Forever players in Australia and New Zealand are struggling to get sunlight, and not for the usual MMO reasons

World of Warcraft: Forever players are having a blast in the new MMO, but not everyone is basking in the rays of its successful launch. Players located in Australia, New Zealand, and other Oceania countries are having a bit of a sunlight problem.

But it's not that too much time behind the computer is keeping WoW players on the other side of the globe away from their precious Vitamin D. Rather, it's in-game sunlight that's scarce for our Oceania friends.

World of Warcraft: Forever, if you didn't already known, has a lovely in-game day/night cycle that aligns with your server clock rather than your local time. So, for a British player, the server time is one hour ahead of GMT. That means if I play during the day I see the sun hanging over Azeroth, and if I do a late night MMO session it's replaced by the moon.

However, while Oceania players can access a data centre in Australia that allows for a solid connection to WoW, they still share the same mega-servers with North Americans. That mega-server is aligned with North American time, differing drastically from Oceania time zones. In other words, for World of Warcraft: Forever players in Oceania, day is night and night is day. And they've had enough!

Reddit user Playful_Artichoke981 has been at the forefront of requests asking Blizzard to address the problem , though they're far from alone. Currently, Oceania players see full daylight in-game from around midnight to 6am in the morning, which obviously is far from normal gaming hours for the majority of players in the region.

"We don't hate the nighttime. We just want variety," writes Playful_Artichoke981. "We don't want to have to compromise our sleep schedules to experience this game in all its glory." Another user, cuddlegoop, echoes the sentiment: "I am totally fine with my day/night changing when I join an NA party. Just let me see the sun! I was up late last night and the view over the bay at Shadowfan Keep in the dawn was so beautiful I want to see stuff like that more often."

Eurogamer has contacted Blizzard to ask if it has plans to address the issue, but we've not received a response at the time of writing.

World of Warcraft: Forever is proving exceptionally popular, breaking records as the biggest launch in the series' history. And based on what I've played this week, it's looking to be a brilliant MMO that's well worth jumping into, if you have the time.

Although Mass Effect 5 is gone thanks to BioWare's closure, we at least have Exodus from Archetype Entertainment, a similar space action-RPG from some of the central devs behind Commander Shepard's iconic adventures. The team is acutely aware of the weight on their shoulders, and they've now revealed who'll voice the protagonist of their romp.

As in the Mass Effect trilogy, you can select your main character's gender. Their name is Jun, and for the male voice, Stephen Oyoung is providing it. You may recognize his dulcet tones from Mister Negative in Marvel's Spider-Man games, but he's also had screen credits in the likes of Mission: Impossible - Final Reckoning and Twisters.

Meanwhile, the female June is performed by Carina Conti, whose biggest video game credit is as Isabella Torrisi from Mafia: The Old Country. Her screen credits, then, include Winning Time and Little Death.

Both fine choices, with strong experience between them. In taking the roles, they're distinctly aware of the expectations on the game.

"We couldn't help but feel the legacy from the very jump," Oyoung tells GamesRadar+. "Especially when you look at the founders of the studio and all of the amazing talent at Archetype, it was foremost certainly in all of our acting cohort's minds that we're definitely engaged in a lineage, and we want to do justice to that."

Indeed, Archetype's senior devs include James Ohlen, Drew Karpyshyn, and Chad Robertson, all former BioWare creatives. It always seemed like Exodus was a spiritual successor to Mass Effect, and now that's doubly so given the circumstances.

"I've heard people say that [Mass Effect] has saved their lives," Conti adds. "It's truly a community rather than a franchise, and so it affects much more than just us. And it's really humbling and exciting and encouraging to think that we could be part of something like that."
